Note.description: A page in the garden — a paper summary, a symptom log, a session note, an index. The only type that owns prose on the site.

Session.description: A dated event in the case: a self-administered test, a therapy conversation, a clinical appointment, a deliberate journalling pass. The unit of 'what we did and when'.

Symptom.description: An experienced pattern being tracked — described phenomenologically, not diagnostically.

Instrument.description: A measurement tool: a screener, a questionnaire, a cognitive task, a lab panel, a wearable metric.

Finding.description: A concrete result produced by a Session — a score, a clinician's observation, a lab value. Facts about the case, distinct from what they might mean.

Intervention.description: Something deliberately changed and tracked over time: medication, sleep protocol, therapy, exercise, caffeine, environment.

Mechanism.description: A named cognitive/neural construct the notebook reuses: response inhibition, statistical learning, mind-wandering, executive function.

Hypothesis.description: A load-bearing assertion the notebook is trying to defend or falsify. Never a diagnosis — always something that can be pressure-tested.

Question.description: An open problem the notebook is working on; can gate a Note, a Hypothesis, or a next Session.

Paper.description: An external work cited: journal article, preprint, book, clinical guideline.

Tension.description: A competing-explanation or trade-off held open on purpose — e.g. ADHD vs. anxiety as the source of the same symptom. Reified so it cannot quietly resolve itself.

Status.description: Lifecycle status (a hub-transit type: reachable but never traversed through).

partOf.description: Note belongs to a parent Note (section index).

covers.description: This note is where the thing is written up.

measures.description: Instrument is designed to measure this symptom domain or construct.

administeredIn.description: Instrument was administered during this session.

observedIn.description: Symptom was reported/observed in this session.

precedes.description: Session comes before another session — the timeline spine.

mayExplain.description: Candidate explanation for an experience or result. HYPOTHETICAL by construction — never a diagnosis.

affects.description: Intervention is being tracked for its effect on this.

derivesFrom.description: X is built on / specialises Y.

documentedIn.description: The case fact is written up in this note.

definedIn.description: Mechanism has its primary development in this note.

cites.description: Note cites a paper (a deliberate act, never inferred from prose).

dependsOn.description: Hypothesis rests on another hypothesis, on a question resolving a particular way, or on a finding holding up.

supports.description: Paper supports this hypothesis/mechanism. The edge carries the verbatim quote + page locator + confidence + rationale, so a fact and its justification travel together.

pressureTests.description: Paper challenges/qualifies this hypothesis/mechanism. Same evidence payload.

confounds.description: A rival explanation that must be ruled out before the hypothesis can stand. The honesty predicate of this ontology.

tensionWith.description: In unresolved tension with (both endpoints stay live).

supersedes.description: Replaces a prior version — later screening supersedes an earlier one, a revised hypothesis supersedes its draft.

flagsOpenQuestion.description: Flags an open question the node rests on.

wikiLinks.description: Wiki-style link parsed from prose. Navigation only — kept out of the argument graph.

structural.description: Where a thing sits: containment, coverage, what measures what.

temporal.description: The case timeline: what happened when, in what order, and what it produced.

causal.description: What might explain or affect what. Always hypothetical in this corpus.

provenance.description: Where a thing came from: which note records it, which paper, which author.

dialectical.description: What is contested: evidence, confounds, contradictions, supersession, open questions.

weak.description: Casual cross-links for navigation only — deliberately kept out of the argument graph.

nodes.label: 2026-07-26 — ASRS v1.1 self-screening & reflection
nodes.summary: Took the ASRS v1.1 (WHO-developed adult ADHD screener) and reflected on presentations and the 'calm outside, churning inside' pattern with a therapist who is themselves diagnosed with ADHD.

nodes.label: ASRS v1.1 (Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale)
nodes.summary: 18-item WHO-developed screener. Part A (6 items, cutoff ≥4) determines the screen; Part B (12 items) characterises symptom load. Deliberately tuned for sensitivity, so a positive screen is a reason to evaluate, not a diagnosis.

nodes.label: Cognitive Trade-off Task (ASRT + Go/No-Go)
nodes.summary: The paradigm used by Horváth et al. 2026: an Alternating Serial Reaction Time Task carrying a hidden probabilistic sequence (statistical learning) with an embedded Go/No-Go component (response inhibition), so both are measured at once rather than in isolation.

nodes.label: Continuous performance test (CPT / QbTest)
nodes.summary: Sustained-attention task requiring responses to targets and withholding to non-targets over a long, monotonous session. Indexes vigilance, inhibition and reaction-time variability; sensitive to ADHD but not diagnostically specific.

nodes.label: Stop-signal / go-no-go task
nodes.summary: Measures the ability to cancel an already-initiated response (the stop-signal reaction time) — the cleanest isolation of response inhibition.

nodes.label: Delay-discounting / choice-delay task
nodes.summary: Choices between smaller-sooner and larger-later rewards, quantifying how steeply delayed value is discounted — the motivational/delay-aversion pathway.

nodes.label: Working-memory task (n-back / span)
nodes.summary: n-back and complex-span paradigms indexing the capacity to hold and manipulate information over short intervals.

nodes.label: SWAN rating scale
nodes.summary: Strengths and Weaknesses of ADHD-symptoms and Normal-behavior scale: rates each symptom on a symmetric −3 to +3 range so both tails are measured, yielding roughly normally distributed population scores.

nodes.label: CAARS (Conners Adult ADHD Rating Scales)
nodes.summary: Norm-referenced adult ADHD rating scale scored as T-scores against a population sample; the T≥65 cutoff trades sensitivity for specificity.

nodes.label: BAARS-IV (Barkley Adult ADHD Rating Scale)
nodes.summary: DSM-anchored adult ADHD rating scale with current and childhood-symptom subscales, self- or observer-administered.

nodes.label: PID-5 (Disinhibition domain)
nodes.summary: Dimensional maladaptive-trait inventory; its Disinhibition domain (and Distractibility facet) places a person on the HiTOP disinhibited-externalizing spectrum rather than in the ADHD category.

nodes.label: Internal Restlessness Scale (IRS)
nodes.summary: Self-report scale (Weyandt et al., 2003) that operationalises the subjective/mental restlessness adults with ADHD report in place of overt motor hyperactivity; four factors — internal distractibility, internal impulsivity, internal restlessness, internal disorganization.

nodes.label: DIVA-5 (Diagnostic Interview for ADHD in Adults)
nodes.summary: Structured clinical interview that walks each DSM ADHD symptom across childhood and adulthood with concrete real-life examples, designed to be supplemented by a collateral informant. The instrument a full evaluation uses — distinct from the ASRS screen — though still a clinician tool, not a stand-alone test.

nodes.label: ASRS v1.1 Part A: 4/6 — positive screen
nodes.summary: Landed exactly at the cutoff on the six-item screener that determines the result. Part A is the most predictive component. Screening only — not a diagnosis.

nodes.label: ASRS v1.1 Part B: 6/12 supplementary symptoms
nodes.summary: Part B has no threshold; it describes which symptoms show up. Six indicates a meaningful additional symptom load, backing the Part A result.

nodes.label: No formal diagnosis as of 2026-07-26
nodes.summary: State of the record: a positive screen only. Everything downstream is hypothesis.

nodes.label: Disruptive internal state — calm outside, churning inside
nodes.summary: Outwardly calm and not fidgety, but a racing, unsettled mind — the DSM 'driven as if by a motor' item experienced mentally rather than behaviourally. The often-missed pattern in inattentive-leaning adults.

nodes.label: Inattentive pattern — sustaining focus, distractibility
nodes.summary: Consistent with a positive ASRS Part A and a lean toward the inattentive presentation.

nodes.label: Acting before thinking / impulsivity items
nodes.summary: Endorsed on the ASRS; the axis the Horváth paper probes directly via response inhibition.

nodes.label: Stimulant medication (methylphenidate / amphetamines)
nodes.summary: First-line pharmacological treatment for ADHD with the largest symptom-reduction effects. Listed here as an option on the table, not a treatment started — nothing is in the personal record. Its diagnostic relevance is a caution: because stimulants improve attention in people without ADHD too, feeling better on a trial would not confirm the diagnosis.

nodes.label: Cognitive behavioural therapy for adult ADHD
nodes.summary: Structured skills-based psychotherapy targeting organisation, planning and impulse control in adults with ADHD; meta-analytic effects comparable to well-established child behavioural treatments. An option on the table, not started.

nodes.label: Mindfulness-based therapy
nodes.summary: Attention-training and acceptance-based practice studied as an adjunct for ADHD, with moderate meta-analytic effects on inattention and hyperactivity/impulsivity. Promising but tentatively evidenced; an option on the table, not started.

nodes.label: Physical exercise (aerobic / cardio)
nodes.summary: Regular aerobic exercise as an evidence-based adjunct for ADHD: meta-analyses show moderate improvements in core symptoms and executive function, acutely and chronically, plausibly via catecholamine upregulation in the same direction as stimulants. Modest and dose-dependent (longer/more consistent helps more), a low-risk complement rather than a replacement. An option on the table, not a tracked protocol.

nodes.label: Dietary modification (elimination diet, omega-3, additive avoidance)
nodes.summary: Dietary approaches to ADHD with modest, variable evidence: restriction/elimination diets help some children (g≈0.29), omega-3 supplementation is modestly effective (below medication), and synthetic-food-color avoidance shows small, bias-prone effects. Not a primary treatment; a low-risk adjunct worth trying with modest expectations for a subgroup. Notably, the sugar-causes-hyperactivity belief is not supported.

nodes.label: Sleep management (sleep hygiene, behavioural intervention, melatonin)
nodes.summary: Improving sleep as a lever on ADHD: sleep hygiene and brief behavioural sleep strategies are guideline first-line for sleep problems and can reduce ADHD symptoms as well as improve sleep; melatonin reliably advances a delayed sleep phase but does not itself treat ADHD symptoms. A low-risk, high-value adjunct given sleep's role in the differential. An option on the table, not a tracked protocol.

nodes.label: Response inhibition
nodes.summary: The capacity to withhold a prepared response — indexed by No-Go accuracy. Consistently weaker at higher ADHD-trait load, even below clinical thresholds.

nodes.label: Statistical learning
nodes.summary: Implicit extraction of environmental regularities — the habit-learning system. Indexed by faster responses to high-probability triplets.

nodes.label: Inhibition–learning antagonism (competition hypothesis)
nodes.summary: The trade-off in which weaker inhibitory control normally buys stronger statistical learning. The paper's central object of study.

nodes.label: ADHD as a trait continuum
nodes.summary: The dimensional view: ADHD-like traits are distributed across the general population, and neurocognitive shifts appear before symptoms reach clinical significance. The frame that makes a screening score meaningful without a diagnosis.

nodes.label: Cue as motivational magnet (sign-tracking)
nodes.summary: Borrowed from animal sign-tracker/goal-tracker work: at high trait load the cue itself captures behaviour and top-down systems cannot override it — the authors' proposed reason the learning advantage breaks down.

nodes.label: Mind-wandering
nodes.summary: Spontaneous shift of attention from external demands to internally generated thought; offered as a second, transdiagnostic candidate mechanism.

nodes.label: Anxiety-driven arousal
nodes.summary: Chronic anxious arousal produces internal churn that is phenomenologically near-identical to internal hyperactivity, and frequently co-occurs with ADHD. The single most important thing to rule out here.

nodes.label: Sleep debt / disrupted sleep
nodes.summary: Insufficient or fragmented sleep degrades attention and produces restlessness — a mimic that must be excluded before attributing symptoms to ADHD.

nodes.label: Mood disturbance (depression / chronic stress)
nodes.summary: Depression and chronic stress produce concentration difficulty and inner agitation. Another mimic on the differential.

nodes.label: Sustained attention / vigilance
nodes.summary: The capacity to maintain attention on a task over time. A mechanism-level axis, indexed by continuous performance tests; lapses show up as reaction-time variability.

nodes.label: Working memory
nodes.summary: Holding and manipulating information over short intervals. One of the dissociable neurocognitive routes to ADHD-like presentation; indexed by n-back and complex-span tasks.

nodes.label: Reward processing / delay aversion
nodes.summary: The motivational pathway: an aversion to waiting and steeper discounting of delayed rewards. Partly independent of the inhibitory route; indexed by delay-discounting paradigms.

nodes.label: Arousal / state regulation
nodes.summary: Regulation of physiological and cognitive arousal. The axis ADHD shares most with its mimics — anxiety, sleep debt and mood all perturb it, which is why they overlap ADHD at the phenotype. The cognitive-energetic model defines its energetic pools as responsive to stress, sleep and noise, so the overlap is by construction; the putatively ADHD-specific part is the regulation, evidenced by condition-dependence.

nodes.label: Excessive spontaneous mind-wandering
nodes.summary: Constant, topic-unstable internal mental activity, proposed to arise from altered default-mode deactivation and DMN–executive interaction. Measured by the MEWS; targets the form rather than the content of thought. Its ADHD-specificity is contested — it also tracks anxiety.

nodes.label: Reaction-time variability
nodes.summary: Intra-individual variability in response speed — a robust and heavily replicated ADHD marker, but not specific to ADHD relative to other clinical groups.

nodes.label: Temporal processing / timing
nodes.summary: Perception and reproduction of time intervals. A third dissociable component in multiple-pathway models, independent of inhibition and delay aversion.

nodes.label: Cognitive disengagement syndrome (formerly sluggish cognitive tempo)
nodes.summary: A construct of attention decoupling from the external context — staring, daydreaming, mental fogginess, slowed thinking and hypoactivity. Distinct from ADHD inattention in factor-analytic work and more strongly tied to internalizing (depression) than to hyperactivity/impulsivity, which makes it a rival reading of a foggy, disengaged 'internal state' rather than an anxious, churning one.

nodes.label: Emotional dysregulation
nodes.summary: Difficulty modulating emotional responses — lability, low frustration tolerance, quick temper, slow return to baseline. Prevalent across the ADHD lifespan and a major driver of impairment, proposed to arise from deficits in attention to emotional stimuli. It overlaps anxiety and mood by construction, so it both deepens the ADHD phenotype and blurs the boundary with the mimics; whether it is core to ADHD or a distinct dimension is unsettled.

nodes.label: Default-mode network interference
nodes.summary: A neurobiological model in which spontaneous low-frequency default-mode-network activity, normally suppressed during tasks, intrudes into task-positive processing and produces periodic attentional lapses. Proposed as a substrate for reaction-time variability and inattention, it links the mind-wandering and vigilance axes to a specific network rather than a single region.

nodes.label: Delayed circadian phase
nodes.summary: A shift of the internal clock later than the day's demands — delayed dim-light melatonin onset, delayed sleep period, chronic sleep-onset insomnia. Distinct from acute sleep debt: it is a rhythm problem, not just a quantity problem. Highly prevalent in ADHD and proposed by some as intrinsic to a subgroup rather than merely comorbid, which is what makes it more than a mimic.

nodes.label: Reproductive-hormone modulation of ADHD symptoms
nodes.summary: Fluctuations in estradiol, progesterone and testosterone across the menstrual cycle (and, by extension, puberty, pregnancy and menopause) modulate ADHD symptom expression in women — lower estradiol tracks worse symptoms. A source of within-person variability specific to females, absent from male-referenced models, and a reason symptom severity can move without the underlying trait changing.

nodes.label: Executive function
nodes.summary: The set of self-regulatory control processes — response inhibition, working memory, sustained attention, planning and self-monitoring — that organise goal-directed behaviour. In leading theory ADHD is a primary executive/inhibition deficit, but empirically EF weakness is neither universal in ADHD nor specific to it, and lab EF tests capture it poorly relative to real-world ratings.

nodes.label: Rejection sensitivity
nodes.summary: A cognitive-affective disposition to anxiously expect, readily perceive, and overreact to social rejection or criticism. A validated general-psychology construct (not ADHD-specific), studied across depression, anxiety and personality disorders; in ADHD it is treated as a facet of emotional dysregulation. Distinct from the popular label 'rejection sensitive dysphoria', which names the same experience but lacks the construct's evidence base.

nodes.label: Hyperfocus / difficulty disengaging attention
nodes.summary: Intense, long-lasting absorption in a task with reduced awareness of surroundings and time, and difficulty shifting attention away from it. Reframes ADHD attention as dysregulated allocation — attention over-deployed as well as under-deployed — rather than a simple deficit. Elevated in ADHD but not specific to it (also invoked for autism and schizophrenia), and still inconsistently defined and measured.

nodes.label: Reward-motivation / reinforcement sensitivity
nodes.summary: How reward and incentive drive behaviour — proposed to be altered in ADHD, with reduced dopamine reward-pathway function and an aberrant sensitivity to reinforcement. Manifests as strongly contingency-dependent performance (reward, interest and urgency lift it) rather than a fixed capacity deficit. Related to but broader than delay aversion, which concerns the timing of reward specifically.

nodes.label: Atypical sensory processing (hyper-/hyposensitivity)
nodes.summary: Over- or under-responsiveness to sensory input — sound, light, texture, touch — and difficulty modulating it. Elevated in ADHD in both directions (hyper and hypo), dimensionally related to ADHD trait level, and present irrespective of autistic symptoms, though it is also a core feature of autism and thus not specific. A plausible contributor to distractibility and to sensory-driven restlessness.

nodes.label: Low self-esteem / negative self-concept
nodes.summary: A negative view of one's own worth and abilities, lower across the ADHD lifespan and on all measured domains. Understood as accumulated rather than intrinsic — built from years of negative feedback, criticism and underperformance — which makes it a plausible link in the demoralization pathway toward depression, and, importantly, remediable rather than fixed.

nodes.label: My disruptive internal state is ADHD-driven rather than anxiety-, sleep-, or mood-driven
nodes.summary: The load-bearing personal hypothesis. Three rival mechanisms confound it and none has been ruled out; it cannot advance until the internal state is described concretely.

nodes.label: My ASRS result places me on the ADHD trait continuum rather than in a yes/no category
nodes.summary: Framing rather than diagnosis: a Part A score at the cutoff situates me somewhere on a spectrum the literature treats dimensionally.

nodes.label: ADHD's latent structure is dimensional (a continuum), not a discrete taxon
nodes.summary: Taxometric analyses of ADHD symptom data repeatedly fail to recover a category boundary and instead fit a continuous latent dimension. Contested: some analyses recover categorical structure within clinical samples.

nodes.label: Clinical ADHD is the quantitative extreme of a continuously distributed, heritable trait
nodes.summary: Twin and molecular-genetic evidence that the same aetiological factors operate across the whole symptom range, so the diagnosis marks a position on a continuum rather than a distinct condition.

nodes.label: The DSM symptom-count threshold is an arbitrary cut on a continuum with no natural breakpoint
nodes.summary: Impairment and quality of life decline linearly across the trait range with no discontinuity, so any diagnostic cutoff is a clinical convention. Held live by the counter-argument that unbounded threshold-lowering risks overdiagnosis and net harm.

nodes.label: Major dimensional frameworks (RDoC, HiTOP, the p-factor) place ADHD within continuous, transdiagnostic spectra
nodes.summary: The leading post-DSM classification programmes are all dimensional and locate ADHD on graded spectra (externalizing/disinhibition, general psychopathology) rather than in a discrete box.

nodes.label: A positive ASRS screen warrants a full clinical evaluation
nodes.summary: The actionable claim. Holds regardless of how the ADHD-vs-mimics question resolves — the evaluation is what resolves it.

nodes.label: Higher ADHD-like traits are associated with weaker response inhibition
nodes.summary: Research-side claim, replicated by the Horváth study in a non-clinical sample and under dual-task load.

nodes.label: Rising ADHD-trait load progressively flattens the inhibition–learning trade-off
nodes.summary: The paper's core result: the compensatory learning advantage that normally accompanies weak inhibition breaks down at the high end of the trait continuum.

nodes.label: Inattention and hyperactivity/impulsivity are distinct but strongly correlated, not orthogonal
nodes.summary: At the phenotype level the two DSM domains share a dominant general factor (latent r ≈ .68–.78); a bifactor structure fits best, so the domains are oblique rather than independent axes.

nodes.label: Rating-based and task-based measures of the same construct are only weakly related
nodes.summary: Questionnaire and performance measures of executive function correlate at about median r = .19 and assess different levels of cognition — so the two instrument families are near-orthogonal, not interchangeable.

nodes.label: ADHD arises through dissociable neurocognitive pathways, present in some individuals but not others
nodes.summary: Inhibitory, delay/reward and timing deficits are independent components whose co-occurrence is no greater than chance, and no single deficit is universal — the mechanism level is genuinely near-orthogonal.

nodes.label: No single instrument is diagnostic; valid assessment is multi-method across levels
nodes.summary: Ratings and tasks disagree, the best objective tasks are not decisive, and robust markers like reaction-time variability are not ADHD-specific — so discriminating ADHD (and its mimics) requires a multi-method evaluation, not one measure.

nodes.label: ADHD measures separate ADHD from healthy controls, but not from the mimics
nodes.summary: Ratings and tasks alike discriminate ADHD from typically developing controls, yet lose their edge against other clinical conditions — anxiety, mood, OCD — so no single instrument can rule out the differential. The measurement-side root of the ADHD-vs-anxiety tension.

nodes.label: Most adult-identified ADHD is late-identified rather than genuinely late-onset
nodes.summary: Birth cohorts found adult and childhood ADHD groups barely overlap, but careful repeated assessment excludes ~95% of screen-positive late-onset cases; survivors show childhood symptoms masked by cognitive strength. Compensation plus rising demand, not new onset.

nodes.label: The course of ADHD fluctuates rather than simply persisting or remitting
nodes.summary: Most of the MTA sample showed waxing and waning persistence and remission rather than stable persistence or recovery, making person-environment fit the appropriate frame — the temporal counterpart of the dimensional argument.

nodes.label: The ADHD sex ratio largely reflects referral and ascertainment, not underlying prevalence
nodes.summary: Clinic ratios far exceed community ratios in the same populations, high-symptom girls are diagnosed less often than high-symptom boys, and the gap narrows to ~1.5:1 in adulthood — the signature of under-detection rather than a true prevalence difference.

nodes.label: The arousal/state-regulation axis is shared with the mimics by construction, not by coincidence
nodes.summary: The cognitive-energetic model defines its energetic pools as responsive to stress, sleep-wake cycle and noise — so sleep debt and anxiety move the very variable ADHD is hypothesised to dysregulate. What may be ADHD-specific is the regulation, evidenced by condition-dependence.

nodes.label: Excessive mind-wandering is transdiagnostic rather than an ADHD marker
nodes.summary: Mind-wandering tracked anxiety independently of ADHD diagnosis and showed no categorical ADHD/non-ADHD difference, while correlating with inattention dimensionally — and it mediates ADHD symptoms' relationship to anxiety and depression.

nodes.label: Sleep debt is a strong rival for inattention but a weak one for internal restlessness
nodes.summary: Experimental sleep restriction reliably degrades attention and emotional lability in healthy people, but no experiment has shown it induces hyperactivity or impulsivity — narrowing which half of the picture sleep can explain.

nodes.label: Onset, trajectory and counterfactual — not symptom intensity — discriminate ADHD from anxiety
nodes.summary: Because both conditions produce internal restlessness and the rating items measuring it are partly anxiety items, the discriminating evidence is structural: whether the restlessness predates any anxiety, persists in its absence, is situational or constant, and whether its content is worry or topic-shifting.

nodes.label: The 'calm outside, churning inside' state is internalized hyperactivity — subjective restlessness — not overt motor hyperactivity
nodes.summary: DSM allows adult hyperactivity to present as subjective restlessness, and adults with ADHD report mental restlessness in place of fidgeting; the IRS measures it and separates ADHD from non-ADHD students. This reframes the internal state as the adult form of the hyperactive axis — but the same internalized presentation is where anxiety is hardest to distinguish from ADHD.

nodes.label: Cognitive disengagement (daydreamy, foggy, mentally slow) is a construct distinct from ADHD inattention and more tied to internalizing
nodes.summary: Factor-analytic and meta-analytic work separates cognitive disengagement syndrome (formerly SCT) from ADHD inattention and links it more to depression/internalizing than to hyperactivity/impulsivity. If the internal state is foggy and disengaged rather than restless, CDS — not ADHD hyperactivity — may be the better description, and it points toward the mood differential.

nodes.label: ADHD and anxiety co-occur far above chance across the lifespan
nodes.summary: Adult ADHD is highly comorbid with other DSM disorders, up to ~80% carry at least one, and ~25% of children with ADHD have an anxiety disorder. High comorbidity is why the ADHD-vs-anxiety differential is genuinely hard rather than a technicality — the two really do travel together.

nodes.label: Emotional dysregulation is a core feature of ADHD, not merely a comorbidity
nodes.summary: Emotion dysregulation is prevalent across the ADHD lifespan and a major contributor to impairment, and has been called a distinctive attribute of adult ADHD. But its status is explicitly unsettled: it is equally consistent with being a correlated-but-distinct dimension or a separate entity, so 'core' is one reading among three.

nodes.label: The DSM childhood-onset requirement is hard to verify from an adult's own recall, so collateral information matters
nodes.summary: DSM needs some symptoms present in childhood, but adult self-recall of childhood ADHD has a positive predictive value near 0.27, and young adults with ADHD tend to underreport. Guidelines therefore lean on contemporaneous records and collateral informants (a parent or partner). This bears directly on a first evaluation in adulthood with no childhood documentation.

nodes.label: A positive response to stimulant medication does not confirm ADHD
nodes.summary: Normal children given dextroamphetamine show the same reduced activity and improved cognition as hyperactive children, so there is no ADHD-specific or 'paradoxical' stimulant response. Improvement on a medication trial is therefore not diagnostic evidence — a treatment-response confound on the personal ADHD hypothesis.

nodes.label: Evidence-based treatments meaningfully reduce adult ADHD symptoms
nodes.summary: Medication (methylphenidate in youth, amphetamines in adults) has the largest short-term effects; CBT for adults reaches effect sizes comparable to well-established child behavioural treatments; mindfulness shows moderate but tentatively-framed benefit. Treatment works — separately from whether a given internal state is ADHD.

nodes.label: ADHD reflects altered function across large-scale brain networks, not a single region or lesion
nodes.summary: The older prefrontal-striatal model has given way to systems-level accounts spanning multiple resting-state networks (frontoparietal, dorsal attention, default, visual). There is no ADHD 'spot' in the brain; the biology is distributed and network-level, which is consistent with a graded, dimensional phenotype rather than a discrete lesion.

nodes.label: Structural brain differences in ADHD are real at the group level but too small to diagnose an individual
nodes.summary: The largest imaging studies (ENIGMA) find real but tiny group differences — subcortical volumes at Cohen's d around -0.1 to -0.2, cortical effects no larger, and no detectable cortical differences at all in adolescents or adults. Group-level signal does not license an individual scan-based diagnosis, and the adult null is especially relevant to a first evaluation in adulthood.

nodes.label: ADHD and autism co-occur far above chance
nodes.summary: Co-occurrence estimates run high (roughly 20–50% of children with ADHD meet ASD criteria and 30–80% of ASD children meet ADHD criteria). DSM-IV had barred diagnosing both, which suppressed research; DSM-5 now permits a dual diagnosis, and the overlap is now openly studied.

nodes.label: ADHD and autism share heritable and neurocognitive substrates
nodes.summary: Family and twin studies support partly shared familial-genetic origins, with candidate pleiotropic genes, and the two share impairments in social and executive functioning. The overlap is not merely superficial symptom sharing but reaches down to partly common causes.

nodes.label: Despite the overlap, ADHD and autism remain distinct diagnostic categories
nodes.summary: Shared genetics and impairments notwithstanding, the phenotypic presentations differ qualitatively and quantitatively enough that reviews conclude the two are sufficiently distinct to warrant separate diagnoses. Overlap at the level of causes does not collapse the clinical distinction.

nodes.label: ADHD and sleep problems are bidirectionally related, not a one-way mimic
nodes.summary: The sleep–ADHD relationship runs both ways and more: sleep loss degrades attention (the mimic direction), while ADHD is associated with markedly disturbed sleep, and the two may share causes. Treating sleep purely as a rival to rule out understates a genuinely multidirectional link.

nodes.label: Delayed circadian phase is highly prevalent in ADHD and may be intrinsic, not merely comorbid
nodes.summary: Delayed sleep phase and delayed melatonin onset appear in most adults with ADHD who have insomnia, and delayed sleep phase disorder is reported in 73–78% of people with ADHD. Some argue part of the symptomatology is a downstream consequence of chronic circadian delay — which would move sleep from mimic to component for a subgroup.

nodes.label: ADHD co-occurs with depression well above chance
nodes.summary: Depression is among the most frequent conditions accompanying ADHD, and people with an ADHD history carry a significantly elevated risk of major depression. The overlap is large enough that low mood and ADHD have to be considered together, not as alternatives.

nodes.label: ADHD is a developmental risk factor for later depression, plausibly causal
nodes.summary: Prospective data show ADHD in adolescence predicts later major depression after adjusting for confounders, and Mendelian-randomization evidence is consistent with a causal effect of ADHD genetic liability on major depression. This reframes some ADHD-plus-depression as ADHD giving rise to depression, not two independent conditions.

nodes.label: Under-identifying ADHD in girls and women is not benign — missed cases carry serious impairment, including elevated self-harm
nodes.summary: Longitudinal follow-up of childhood-diagnosed girls shows persistent impairment and markedly elevated suicide attempts and self-injury into early adulthood, and reviews single out self-harm as a heightened risk for females with ADHD. The under-recognition documented elsewhere therefore has real stakes, not merely epidemiological ones.

nodes.label: ADHD symptom expression in women fluctuates with reproductive hormones
nodes.summary: Within-person, ADHD symptoms in regularly-cycling women rise when estradiol falls relative to progesterone or testosterone, peaking in specific menstrual phases. Symptom severity can thus move with the hormonal cycle independently of the underlying trait — a female-specific source of variability that male-referenced criteria and single-timepoint assessments miss.

nodes.label: A leading theory casts ADHD as fundamentally a deficit in behavioral inhibition, from which other executive functions follow
nodes.summary: Barkley's unifying model makes behavioral inhibition the primary deficit and derives working memory, self-regulation of affect/motivation, internalized speech and reconstitution from it. Influential and organising, but the author cautions it needs far more testing — and the empirical record (see the necessary-nor-sufficient hypothesis) complicates a single-core-deficit reading.

nodes.label: Executive-function deficits are real and central in ADHD on average, but neither necessary nor sufficient
nodes.summary: Meta-analysis finds significant EF impairment across all domains (medium effect sizes, strongest for inhibition, vigilance, working memory, planning), yet the deficits are not universal among people with ADHD and not specific to it. EF weakness is one important component of a heterogeneous neuropsychology, not the defining lesion — consistent with the multiple-pathways view.

nodes.label: 'Rejection sensitive dysphoria' is a popular but under-validated label for a real, established phenomenon
nodes.summary: RSD spread through social media and clinical anecdote (coined by Dodson) rather than through validation studies, and critical appraisal flags limited empirical evidence plus risks of stigma and reifying it as innate. The experience it names is real and better captured by the established rejection-sensitivity construct — so the phenomenon is genuine even though the specific ADHD-syndrome label is not well grounded.

nodes.label: Heightened rejection sensitivity is an under-explored facet of ADHD-related emotional dysregulation
nodes.summary: Rejection sensitivity is treated as one aspect of the emotional dysregulation that is prevalent and impairing in ADHD, but the ADHD-specific evidence is thin — small, mostly qualitative studies. Plausible and clinically resonant, not yet firmly established, and not specific to ADHD (rejection sensitivity also marks depression, anxiety and personality disorders).

nodes.label: Hyperfocus is more prevalent in ADHD and may be a separable feature of the syndrome
nodes.summary: On new self-report measures, hyperfocus rises with ADHD symptomology and is higher in adult ADHD than controls, independent of stimulant use, prompting proposals that it is a separable dimension of ADHD. The evidence is young — new questionnaires, small-to-moderate samples — and hyperfocus is inconsistently defined and not specific to ADHD, so the claim is emerging rather than settled.

nodes.label: ADHD is better understood as dysregulated attention allocation than as a simple deficit of attention
nodes.summary: That the same people who cannot sustain attention on demand can also become unable to disengage from an absorbing task points to a regulation problem — attention deployed in the wrong amounts at the wrong times — rather than a straightforward shortage of attention. Hyperfocus is the over-deployed pole of that dysregulation.

nodes.label: ADHD is associated with consistent deficits in perceiving and reproducing time
nodes.summary: Reviews find ADHD consistently impaired across timing domains — motor timing, perceptual timing (duration discrimination and reproduction) and temporal foresight — from milliseconds to long intervals, alongside the lived sense that time slips away. Robust as a group-level finding; the felt 'time blindness' has a real cognitive basis.

nodes.label: Impaired time perception has been proposed as a possible diagnostic characteristic of ADHD
nodes.summary: Some reviews propose time-perception impairment as a candidate diagnostic feature of ADHD. But timing deficits are not specific to ADHD (they occur in other conditions), the measures and paradigms are heterogeneous, and the evidence needs replication — so the marker claim is a proposal, not an established diagnostic test.

nodes.label: Beyond attention and impulsivity, ADHD involves a motivation/reward-processing difference tied to the dopamine reward pathway
nodes.summary: There is increasing evidence of motivation deficits in ADHD, with PET data linking lower trait motivation to reduced dopamine reward-pathway function, and reviews casting an aberrant sensitivity to reinforcement as a core deficit. Motivation is a third axis alongside inattention and hyperactivity/impulsivity, not just willpower.

nodes.label: ADHD performance is strongly modulated by reinforcement, so it reflects reward-dependent regulation rather than fixed incapacity
nodes.summary: Reinforcement contingencies improve task performance and motivation in ADHD (somewhat more than in controls), and immediate reward is preferred to delayed. Being able to perform well when a task is interesting, urgent or rewarded — and poorly when it is not — is a reward-processing signature, not laziness or a stable inability.

nodes.label: Working-memory deficits are large, robust, central to ADHD models, and persist into adulthood
nodes.summary: Meta-analyses find working memory a prominent candidate primary deficit/endophenotype in ADHD, with large between-group effects (larger for spatial than verbal), independent of comorbidity and IQ, and persisting from childhood into adulthood. One of the most consistently replicated cognitive findings in ADHD — though, like other executive measures, not on its own diagnostic.

nodes.label: Excess movement in ADHD may be partly compensatory — aiding working memory rather than only impairing
nodes.summary: When gross motor activity was measured during working-memory tasks, higher activity predicted better working-memory performance in children with ADHD (but worse in typically developing children). This reframes at least some hyperactivity and restlessness as a compensatory mechanism recruited to support cognition, not purely a symptom to suppress.

nodes.label: Atypical sensory sensitivity (hyper- and hypo-) is elevated in ADHD and tracks ADHD traits dimensionally
nodes.summary: Adults and children with ADHD report more sensory hyper- and hyposensitivity than norm groups, and in the general population sensory difficulty rises with ADHD-trait level (a dose-response, all-modalities relationship). Consistent across clinical and non-clinical samples, fitting the trait-continuum view.

nodes.label: Sensory difficulties may be part of the ADHD phenotype itself, not merely autism comorbidity
nodes.summary: Sensory atypicality is a core feature of autism, and ADHD and autism co-occur — but atypical sensory profiles appear in adult ADHD irrespective of autistic symptoms, and general-population data suggest sensory difficulty could be part of the ADHD phenotype. The area remains under-studied and questionnaire-based, so this is emerging rather than settled.

nodes.label: In ADHD, comorbidity is the rule rather than the exception
nodes.summary: Most adults with ADHD carry at least one co-occurring psychiatric disorder — anxiety, mood, substance use, personality, autism, sleep and learning disorders foremost. This makes the differential usually a matter of 'and', not 'or': the question is rarely ADHD versus one rival but which conditions co-occur and how they interact.

nodes.label: ADHD elevates risk for substance use disorders, and is over-represented among people with SUD
nodes.summary: Prospective follow-up shows childhood ADHD predicts later abuse/dependence across nicotine, alcohol, marijuana and cocaine, and about a quarter of substance-use-disorder patients meet criteria for ADHD. The relationship runs both ways, making substance use a comorbidity worth screening for on either side.

nodes.label: ADHD is associated with lower self-esteem across the lifespan, built from accumulated negative feedback
nodes.summary: Children, adolescents and adults with ADHD score lower on self-esteem than controls, across domains and over long-term follow-up. The leading account is not that ADHD directly lowers self-worth but that growing up with negative messages, criticism and repeated underperformance erodes it — a consequence, not a core symptom.

nodes.label: Low self-esteem in ADHD is not fixed — it improves with treatment and support
nodes.summary: Self-esteem difficulties in ADHD respond to intervention: long-term outcome reviews find treatment associated with improvement in most self-esteem outcomes, and psychotherapeutic work can at least partly remedy them. The negative self-concept is a modifiable consequence, which matters for how the whole picture is framed.

nodes.label: ADHD is associated with poorer couple and family relationship quality, including higher divorce risk
nodes.summary: Adults with ADHD report poorer marital adjustment and family functioning, ADHD symptom levels predict lower romantic relationship quality, and parents raising a child with ADHD divorce more and sooner. The strain runs through both the couple (an adult partner's ADHD) and the family (parenting an ADHD child).

nodes.label: The relationship impact of ADHD is partly mediated by emotional dysregulation and conflict
nodes.summary: The link between ADHD symptoms and lower relationship quality is not direct: emotion-regulation problems and hostile conflict carry much of it. This ties relationship difficulty back to the emotional-dysregulation axis rather than to inattention alone, and points to what treatment might target.

nodes.label: The observable couple-conflict signature of ADHD is concentrated in the combined presentation, not inattentive-only
nodes.summary: When couples' conflict behaviour is coded directly, combined-type ADHD couples show more negativity and less positivity — tracking lower satisfaction — while inattentive-type couples look much like non-diagnosed couples. This locates the visible relational damage in the hyperactive-impulsive/combined phenotype and complicates a simple 'inattention strains relationships' account, though it rests on a single observational study.

nodes.label: Sexual dysfunction is markedly more prevalent in adults with ADHD than in the general population
nodes.summary: In a clinical ADHD sample, roughly four in ten adults screened positive for a sexual dysfunction — far above general-population rates — and such problems were almost never previously diagnosed. An under-recognised strand of intimacy and relationship difficulty, and an argument for screening sexual functioning during ADHD assessment. Rests so far on one clinic sample against population norms.

nodes.label: Physical (especially aerobic) exercise improves ADHD symptoms and executive function, acutely and chronically
nodes.summary: Meta-analyses and reviews find aerobic/cardio exercise produces moderate improvements in core ADHD symptoms (attention, hyperactivity, impulsivity) and in executive functions, with both acute post-bout effects and chronic effects of sustained training. A genuine, replicated behavioural benefit — plausibly catecholaminergic, in the same direction as medication.

nodes.label: The exercise benefit for ADHD is modest and dose-dependent — an adjunct, not a replacement
nodes.summary: Pooled effects on functional outcomes are modest (around g=0.6) and grow with longer intervention duration rather than intensity, so exercise complements rather than substitutes for other treatment. Real and worth doing, but not a stand-alone fix, and mostly studied in children.

nodes.label: The popular belief that sugar causes hyperactivity is not supported
nodes.summary: Blinded, placebo-controlled sugar-challenge studies find no effect of sugar on children's behaviour or cognition; the widespread parental conviction is attributed to expectancy and coincidental association. One of the most entrenched ADHD folk beliefs, and a false one.

nodes.label: Dietary interventions have small, variable effects on ADHD — helpful for some, not a primary treatment
nodes.summary: Restriction/elimination diets, food-color avoidance and omega-3 supplementation all show small effect sizes that benefit subgroups rather than everyone, with food-color effects especially bias-prone. Reasonable low-risk adjuncts with modest expectations, not a substitute for evaluation and standard treatment.

nodes.label: The association between screen/media use and ADHD-related behaviors is statistically small
nodes.summary: Across a meta-analysis (r+ = .12), a four-decade review, and a prospective cohort, screen media use is only weakly related to ADHD-related behaviors. The link is real but modest — far from the strong causal story of public worry.

nodes.label: Whether screen use causes ADHD is unresolved, and the relationship is plausibly bidirectional
nodes.summary: Even the prospective evidence stops short of causation, and reviews call explicitly for causal research. Reverse causation is plausible: ADHD-related reward-seeking and need for stimulation may drive intense screen use as much as the reverse, so screens may be an expression of the trait as well as a possible contributor.

nodes.label: Procrastination is strongly linked to ADHD — clinically central though not a formal criterion — driven especially by inattention
nodes.summary: Procrastination is routinely targeted in ADHD psychotherapy but is not an official DSM symptom; where studied, it correlates with ADHD-related behaviour, and specifically with inattention rather than impulsivity once the two are separated. A near-universal ADHD complaint that the diagnostic criteria do not name.

nodes.label: Procrastination is a self-regulation and delay-discounting failure, not a time-management flaw
nodes.summary: Procrastination is best understood as failure of self-regulation and volition — predicted by executive-function weaknesses and by impulsiveness, distractibility and task-delay, and captured by temporal-motivation/hyperbolic-discounting models. That profile is precisely ADHD's, so ADHD is the extreme of the procrastination-prone temperament rather than a separate story.

nodes.label: ADHD carries substantial stigma across the lifespan, driven largely by public doubt about the disorder’s validity
nodes.summary: People with ADHD symptoms of all ages face substantial stigma, prejudice and discrimination, and the most frequent stereotype is doubt about whether ADHD is a real disorder. The stigma rests substantially on a factual question the dimensional, genetic and neurobiological evidence in this notebook already answers.

nodes.label: Internalized stigma and anticipated discrimination are prevalent in adults with ADHD and add to the burden of disease
nodes.summary: A large fraction of adults with ADHD internalize stigma and anticipate discrimination, and these correlate with symptoms, distress, lower self-esteem, impairment and reduced quality of life. Stigma is not just an external attitude but a measurable added load carried by the person.

nodes.label: Improving sleep (behavioural sleep intervention / sleep hygiene) reduces ADHD symptoms, not just sleep problems
nodes.summary: A brief behavioural sleep intervention in children with ADHD reduced ADHD symptom severity and sleep problems, with part of the symptom benefit mediated through improved sleep; guidelines make healthy sleep practices the first-line response to sleep problems. Sleep is thus a genuinely modifiable lever on daytime symptoms, not only a comorbidity.

nodes.label: Melatonin reliably advances sleep onset and circadian phase in ADHD but does not directly improve ADHD symptoms
nodes.summary: In a randomised trial, melatonin advanced sleep onset and dim-light melatonin onset and increased total sleep, but had no significant effect on behaviour, cognition or quality of life. It targets the delayed body clock, which matters given the circadian delay common in ADHD, but is a sleep treatment rather than an ADHD treatment.

nodes.label: CBT-taught coping and self-management skills reduce ADHD symptoms, even in medicated adults
nodes.summary: A skills-based CBT (organisation, planning, coping, cognitive restructuring) added to stable medication lowered clinician- and self-rated ADHD symptoms and global severity relative to medication alone. Learnable coping strategies are an evidence-based lever that adds to, rather than merely substitutes for, other treatment.

nodes.label: Compensatory coping in ADHD works but is effortful, and its long-term quality-of-life payoff is uneven
nodes.summary: Adults with ADHD lean on effortful strategies — routine and habit, reframing, symptom-specific tactics — and simply must work harder than peers to keep up; yet the long-term quality-of-life benefit of coping-focused CBT was not confirmed. Coping reduces symptoms more reliably than it lifts life quality, and the effort itself is a cost worth naming.

nodes.label: Sex-hormone fluctuations modulate ADHD symptoms and cognition across the female lifespan
nodes.summary: Estrogen and related steroids regulate the neurotransmitter and signalling systems implicated in ADHD, so symptom expression can shift with the menstrual cycle and, by extension, across puberty, pregnancy/postpartum and perimenopause. A female-specific source of variability that male-referenced models and single-timepoint assessment miss.

nodes.label: Hormone-related mood conditions (PMDD, postpartum depression, climacteric symptoms) are more prevalent in women with ADHD
nodes.summary: Across reproductive transitions, women with ADHD report premenstrual dysphoric disorder and postpartum depression symptoms more often than the general population, plus elevated climacteric mood and somatic complaints. The hormonal sensitivity of ADHD shows up not just as symptom fluctuation but as raised risk of hormone-linked mood disorders.

nodes.label: The ADHD-creativity link is real but nuanced: a divergent-thinking advantage at trait level, for idea generation, not the clinical disorder or convergent thinking
nodes.summary: Increased divergent thinking (idea generation) is found mainly for high ADHD traits (subclinical) rather than the clinical disorder, with no advantage in convergent thinking (refining to one right answer), and stimulants do not overall reduce creativity. So the popular 'ADHD = creativity' claim is partly true but specific — a trait-level, idea-generation effect, not a superpower conferred by the disorder.

nodes.label: Real-world creative achievement is elevated in ADHD and driven by goal-directed motivation in self-selected domains
nodes.summary: Creative abilities and achievements are high in ADHD, and experimental work links this to goal-directed motivation (more original ideas when competing for a reward) and to selectively engaging domains that fit one's skills and interests. Creativity flourishes where interest and reward align — the reward-motivation account applied to a strength rather than a deficit.

nodes.label: Impulsivity in ADHD is not one thing but several dissociable facets with different biological bases
nodes.summary: Impulsivity fractionates into distinct components — motor/response inhibition (stop-signal), choice impulsivity (delay discounting), and emotional urgency — measured by different paradigms and with different neural substrates, and it sits within a broader self-regulation spanning action, emotion and cognition. A person can show one facet strongly and another not at all, consistent with the dissociable-pathways view.

nodes.label: Impulsivity is transdiagnostic — it describes ADHD but does not distinguish it
nodes.summary: Impulsivity is a component of many conditions (ADHD, mania, substance use), and stop-signal inhibition deficits appear in ADHD, OCD and schizophrenia at comparable magnitude. So 'impulsive' is a real feature of ADHD but a shared one — it characterises without discriminating.

nodes.label: What does the 'disruptive internal state' actually consist of?
nodes.summary: Racing/jumping thoughts, a physical-but-invisible wound-up feeling, an inability to ever relax, or something else. These feel similar from the inside but point in different directions.
nodes.nextStep: Journal concrete examples as they happen, with time of day and context.

nodes.label: Is the internal restlessness driven by ADHD, anxiety, sleep, mood, or a combination?
nodes.summary: The differential. A good evaluator traces the symptom to its source rather than assuming the ADHD thread.
nodes.nextStep: Bring the differential explicitly to the evaluation; don't let it collapse into a single label.
