nodes.summary: The paper's sample scored M = 31.66, SD = 10.04 on the 18-item ASRS. My record currently stores Part A/Part B counts, not the summed dimensional score — so the comparison can't yet be made.
nodes.nextStep: Retain the item-level ASRS responses and compute the summed score.

nodes.label: What is the right next clinical step, and with whom?
nodes.summary: GP referral, psychologist, or psychiatrist — and what to bring to make the appointment productive.
nodes.nextStep: Draft a one-page summary for a clinician from the diagnostics note and the symptom log.

nodes.label: What actually strengthens the relationships of adults with ADHD?
nodes.summary: Reviews note the couple-level impairment is well documented but that little research identifies the factors that would strengthen or repair these relationships, so couple- and emotion-regulation-focused intervention evidence is thin — leaving 'treat the emotional-regulation piece' better supported in principle than in trials.
nodes.nextStep: Raise relationship strain and the emotion-regulation route explicitly at an evaluation; consider couple-oriented or emotion-regulation-focused support alongside standard treatment.

nodes.label: ADHD-like traits reshape the balance between inhibitory control and predictive processes
nodes.summary: n = 226 non-clinical sample; Cognitive Trade-off Task measuring response inhibition and statistical learning simultaneously; ADHD traits measured dimensionally with the ASRS v1.1.

nodes.label: Annual Research Review: Categories versus dimensions in the classification and conceptualisation of child and adolescent mental disorders
nodes.venue: Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry, 53(5):469–489
nodes.summary: Canonical review of the category-vs-dimension question in child psychopathology; summarises the ADHD taxometric studies (Haslam 2006, Marcus & Barry 2011) and concludes ADHD is best modelled as a continuum.

nodes.label: Understanding attention deficit hyperactivity disorder as a continuum
nodes.summary: Clinician-facing review arguing ADHD lacks a taxon; neuropsychological performance varies linearly with symptom load with no discontinuity, creating uncertainty about where any intervention threshold should sit.

nodes.label: Does Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder Have a Dimensional Latent Structure? A Taxometric Analysis
nodes.summary: Taxometric analysis of the NICHD sample finding a dimensional latent structure for inattention, hyperactivity/impulsivity and ADHD overall, with stronger validity than dichotomous models.

nodes.label: Genetics of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder
nodes.summary: Review of ADHD genetics; twin and molecular evidence that clinical ADHD is the extreme of a continuous, heritable distribution with shared aetiology across the full symptom range.

nodes.label: Discovery of the first genome-wide significant risk loci for attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder
nodes.summary: First well-powered ADHD GWAS; strong concordance with GWAS of quantitative population symptom measures supports clinical ADHD as an extreme expression of continuous heritable traits.

nodes.label: The World Health Organization Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale (ASRS): a short screening scale for use in the general population
nodes.summary: Development of the ASRS; optimal scoring is an unweighted symptom sum (a dimensional score), with a 6-item Part A retained as a fast screener.

nodes.label: SWAN Scale for ADHD Trait-Based Genetic Research: A Validity and Polygenic Risk Study
nodes.venue: Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry, 60(9):988–997
nodes.summary: Validates the SWAN, a symmetric strengths-to-weaknesses rating that yields roughly normally distributed ADHD-trait scores; argues dichotomising a continuous trait into case/control loses statistical power.

nodes.label: The Factor Structure of ADHD – Different Models, Analyses and Informants in a Bifactor Framework
nodes.venue: Journal of Psychopathology and Behavioral Assessment, 39(1):92–102
nodes.summary: Supports a bifactor structure for ADHD: a dominant general factor plus weak specific inattention and hyperactivity/impulsivity factors.

nodes.label: Research Domain Criteria (RDoC): Toward a New Classification Framework for Research on Mental Disorders
nodes.summary: Founding RDoC commentary; reorganises psychopathology around functional dimensions studied across their full range, including executive- and impulse-control constructs central to ADHD.

nodes.label: The Hierarchical Taxonomy of Psychopathology (HiTOP): A Dimensional Alternative to Traditional Nosologies
nodes.summary: Dimensional classification framework that places ADHD within the (disinhibited) externalizing super-spectrum rather than as a discrete category.

nodes.label: The p Factor: One General Psychopathology Factor in the Structure of Psychiatric Disorders?
nodes.summary: Finds psychopathology is best captured by a single general 'p' dimension paralleling g; ADHD loads via the externalizing pole, reinforcing a graded liability model.

nodes.label: Is ADHD a Dimension or a Category? What Does the Relationship Between ADHD Traits and Psychosocial Quality of Life Tell Us?
nodes.summary: Psychosocial quality of life declines linearly with ADHD-trait level, with no non-linear breakpoint at the high end — direct support for a dimensional model over a category.

nodes.label: Subthreshold Autism and ADHD: A Brief Narrative Review for Frontline Clinicians
nodes.summary: Narrative review synthesising taxometric, impairment and threshold evidence; documents that sub-threshold ADHD carries wide-ranging functional impairment relative to unaffected peers.

nodes.label: Overdiagnosis of Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder in Children and Adolescents: A Systematic Scoping Review
nodes.summary: Scoping review of 334 studies finding convincing evidence that ADHD is overdiagnosed; for milder cases the harms of diagnosis may outweigh the benefits — a caution against unbounded threshold-lowering.

nodes.label: Childhood attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder as an extreme of a continuous trait: a quantitative genetic study of 8,500 twin pairs
nodes.venue: Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry, 53(1):73–80
nodes.summary: Flagship twin study reporting near-identical group heritability at diagnostic and screening cutoffs — ADHD as the quantitative extreme of a continuous trait.

nodes.label: Dimensional and Categorical Approaches to Understanding Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder: New Frontiers in Translational Research
nodes.venue: Biological Psychiatry: Cognitive Neuroscience and Neuroimaging, 3(8):652–653
nodes.summary: Counter-point to the dimensional consensus: reports taxometric outcomes more consistent with a categorical structure within ADHD samples and a dimensional structure in typically developing groups.

nodes.label: The factor structure of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder in schoolchildren
nodes.venue: medRxiv preprint (later Research in Developmental Disabilities)
nodes.summary: Reports the latent correlation between the inattention and hyperactivity/impulsivity factors (0.78 school / 0.68 clinical) and finds a bifactor model — strong general factor plus weak specific factors — fits best.

nodes.label: Practitioner Review: Do performance-based measures and ratings of executive function assess the same construct?
nodes.venue: Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry, 54(2):131–143
nodes.summary: Review of 20 studies finding rating-based and performance-based measures of executive function correlate only weakly (median r = .19) and assess different underlying constructs.

nodes.label: Causal heterogeneity in attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder: do we need neuropsychologically impaired subtypes?
nodes.summary: Argues that group neuropsychological deficits in ADHD reflect only a subgroup — for any given mechanism, only a subset of behaviourally defined cases is impaired.

nodes.label: Beyond the dual pathway model: evidence for the dissociation of timing, inhibitory, and delay-related impairments in ADHD
nodes.venue: Journal of the American Academy of Child & Adolescent Psychiatry, 49(4):345–355
nodes.summary: Finds inhibitory, temporal-processing and delay-related deficits are independent neuropsychological components whose co-occurrence in ADHD is no greater than chance — dissociable pathways.

nodes.label: Reaction time variability in ADHD: a meta-analytic review of 319 studies
nodes.summary: Meta-analysis establishing greater reaction-time variability in ADHD (g = 0.76 children, 0.46 adults) while showing it is not specific to ADHD relative to other clinical groups.

nodes.label: The clinical utility of the continuous performance test and objective measures of activity for diagnosing and monitoring ADHD in children: a systematic review
nodes.summary: Systematic review finding mixed, non-decisive evidence for using continuous performance tests to support ADHD diagnosis and medication decisions.

nodes.label: A review of the validity of laboratory cognitive tasks used to assess symptoms of ADHD
nodes.summary: Concludes that even the best-supported cognitive tasks (CPT, choice-delay, stop-signal) need further validation before use beyond experimental purposes.

nodes.label: Validity of the executive function theory of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder: a meta-analytic review
nodes.summary: Landmark meta-analysis: executive-function deficits in ADHD are of moderate effect size and not universal — neither necessary nor sufficient.

nodes.label: A comprehensive assessment of memory, delay aversion, timing, inhibition, decision making and variability in ADHD
nodes.summary: For each cognitive domain, only a minority of children with ADHD (roughly 18–36%) show a deficit — quantifying neurocognitive heterogeneity across six pathways.

nodes.label: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder and Monetary Delay Discounting: A Meta-Analysis of Case-Control Studies
nodes.venue: Biological Psychiatry: Cognitive Neuroscience and Neuroimaging, 1(4):316–325
nodes.summary: Meta-analysis finding individuals with ADHD discount delayed monetary rewards more steeply than controls — the motivational/reward pathway.

nodes.label: A review of behavioural rating scales for the assessment of ADHD among adults in research
nodes.summary: Reviews adult ADHD rating scales (incl. CAARS, BAARS-IV); notes scales should not be the sole basis for diagnosis and that combining interviews, CPTs and scales maximises accuracy.

nodes.label: Diagnosing ADHD
nodes.venue: CHADD — National Resource Center on ADHD (CDC cooperative agreement)
nodes.summary: Patient-facing clinical guidance stating there is no single test for ADHD and that a comprehensive, multi-source evaluation is required.

nodes.label: Unraveling the optimum latent structure of ADHD: evidence supporting ICD and HiTOP frameworks
nodes.summary: Locates ADHD within HiTOP as dimensions (inattention, hyperactivity, impulsivity) under the disinhibited externalizing spectrum rather than as a single category.

nodes.label: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis: Clinical Utility of Continuous Performance Tests for the Identification of ADHD
nodes.venue: Journal of the American Academy of Child & Adolescent Psychiatry, 63(2):154–171
nodes.summary: Meta-analysis: CPTs differentiate ADHD from non-ADHD only modestly (pooled sensitivity 0.75, specificity 0.71) and should be used only within a comprehensive diagnostic process.

nodes.label: ADHD and behavioral inhibition: a meta-analytic review of the stop-signal paradigm
nodes.summary: Meta-analysis finding that stop-signal differences in ADHD reflect a generalized attention/processing deficit rather than a specific behavioural-inhibition failure.

nodes.label: Are we measuring ADHD or anxiety? Examining the factor structure and discriminant validity of the ASRS in an adult anxiety disorder population
nodes.summary: In an adult anxiety sample, several ASRS hyperactivity items loaded more strongly onto anxiety than ADHD; the scale captured non-ADHD symptoms and is susceptible to over-reporting.

nodes.label: Is adult ADHD a childhood-onset neurodevelopmental disorder? Evidence from a four-decade longitudinal cohort study
nodes.summary: Dunedin birth cohort: childhood-ADHD and adult-ADHD groups were virtually non-overlapping, and the adult group showed neither childhood neuropsychological deficits nor polygenic risk for childhood ADHD.

nodes.label: Evaluation of the persistence, remission, and emergence of ADHD in young adulthood
nodes.summary: E-Risk twin cohort: 67.5% of young adults with ADHD had never met criteria in childhood; the late-onset group had higher childhood IQ and fewer externalizing problems.

nodes.label: ADHD trajectories from childhood to young adulthood: evidence from a birth cohort supporting a late-onset syndrome
nodes.summary: Pelotas birth cohort: only 17.2% of childhood cases persisted and only 12.6% of adult cases had childhood ADHD; the authors propose two syndromes with distinct trajectories.

nodes.label: Late-onset ADHD reconsidered with comprehensive repeated assessments between ages 10 and 25
nodes.summary: Using eight repeated multi-informant assessments, ~95% of screen-positive late-onset cases were excluded on careful diagnosis; survivors are reframed as late-identified rather than late-onset.

nodes.label: Variable patterns of remission from ADHD in the Multimodal Treatment Study of ADHD
nodes.summary: Across 16 years, only 9.1% recovered and 10.8% were stably persistent; 63.8% showed fluctuating persistence and remission, motivating a person-environment fit framework.

nodes.label: ADHD in DSM-5: a field trial in a large, representative sample of 18- to 19-year-old adults
nodes.summary: Supports five inattention symptoms as the optimal adult cut-off while estimating a 27% increase in expected young-adult prevalence from DSM-IV to DSM-5.

nodes.label: The prevalence of adult attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder: a global systematic review and meta-analysis
nodes.summary: Persistent adult ADHD 2.58% vs symptomatic adult ADHD 6.76% — a ~2.6x difference driven purely by whether childhood onset is required; both decline with age.

nodes.label: ADHD diagnosis, treatment, and telehealth use in adults — National Center for Health Statistics Rapid Surveys System
nodes.venue: MMWR Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report, 73(40):890–895
nodes.summary: 6.0% of US adults had a current ADHD diagnosis in 2023; 55.9% were diagnosed at age 18 or older — late identification is the majority pathway.

nodes.label: Sex and age differences in ADHD symptoms and diagnoses: implications for DSM-V and ICD-11
nodes.venue: Journal of the American Academy of Child & Adolescent Psychiatry, 49(3):217–228
nodes.summary: Community-ascertained male:female ratio of 2.28:1, well below clinic-based ratios, indicating females are underdiagnosed in the community.

nodes.label: Sex differences in predicting ADHD clinical diagnosis and pharmacological treatment
nodes.summary: Swedish cohort: diagnosed ratio 2.5:1 vs symptom-criteria ratio 1.8:1; externalizing behaviour drives referral, and females are missed without it.

nodes.label: Annual Research Review: ADHD in girls and women — underrepresentation, longitudinal processes, and key directions
nodes.venue: Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry, 63(4):484–496
nodes.summary: Reviews presentation differences, the narrowing adult sex ratio, compensation/masking, and the male-referenced bias of ADHD symptom lists.

nodes.label: The prevalence of DSM-IV attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder: a meta-analytic review
nodes.summary: The inattentive presentation is most common in the population, but combined-type individuals are more likely to be referred for services — a structural referral filter.

nodes.label: Gender differences in objective and subjective measures of ADHD among clinic-referred children
nodes.summary: Documents the 2:1 to 10:1 range of reported sex ratios and that higher ratios come specifically from clinical rather than population-based samples.

nodes.label: Bias by gender: exploring gender-based differences in the endorsement of ADHD symptoms and impairment among adult patients
nodes.summary: Notes that only 21% of participants in the DSM-5/ICD-11 ADHD field trials were girls, so diagnostic tools were largely not designed with women in mind.

nodes.label: Modeling attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder: a critical appraisal of the cognitive-energetic model
nodes.summary: Argues inhibition deficits in ADHD may be partly explained by energetic (activation/effort) dysfunction, while conceding the model needs direct measures of the energetic pools.

nodes.label: A comparison of two models of ADHD: state regulation versus delay aversion
nodes.venue: Doctoral dissertation, Ghent University (ch. based on Metin et al. 2012, Biological Psychiatry 72:990–996)
nodes.summary: Meta-analysis of event-rate effects showing ADHD performance deficits are condition-dependent; also states that the energetic pools are affected by stress, sleep-wake cycle and noise.

nodes.label: Arousal dysregulation and executive dysfunction in attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD)
nodes.summary: Reviews evidence that the ADHD impairment is in the ability to self-regulate arousal rather than a constant under- or over-aroused state, while noting mixed results.

nodes.label: Mind wandering perspective on attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder
nodes.summary: Proposes that altered default-mode deactivation and DMN–executive interaction produce excessive spontaneous mind-wandering underpinning ADHD symptoms.

nodes.label: Validation of the Mind Excessively Wandering Scale and the relationship of mind wandering to impairment in adult ADHD
nodes.summary: Validates the MEWS (sensitivity .9, specificity .9) and finds mind-wandering contributes to impairment independently of core ADHD symptom dimensions.

nodes.label: Mind-wandering, depression, anxiety and ADHD: disentangling the relationship
nodes.summary: Found no mind-wandering difference between ADHD and non-ADHD groups; mind-wandering tracked anxiety instead and 'cannot be considered a hallmark of ADHD'.

nodes.label: Associations of sleep disturbance with ADHD: implications for treatment
nodes.venue: ADHD Attention Deficit and Hyperactivity Disorders, 7(1):1–18
nodes.summary: Sets out four modes of ADHD-sleep interaction including that sleep problems may cause or mimic ADHD, and notes no experiment has shown sleep restriction induces hyperactivity.

nodes.label: Impact of sleep extension and restriction on children's emotional lability and impulsivity
nodes.summary: In healthy children with no sleep or behavioural problems, ~54 minutes of cumulative sleep restriction produced detectable deterioration on blinded teacher ratings.

nodes.label: Sleep restriction and extension in adolescents with ADHD
nodes.venue: Journal of the American Academy of Child & Adolescent Psychiatry, 58(4):433–442
nodes.summary: Experimental evidence that sleep duration is a causal contributor to daytime behaviour in adolescents with ADHD; hyperactivity-impulsivity was lower under restriction.

nodes.label: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) in adults: evidence base, uncertainties and controversies
nodes.summary: Comprehensive review of adult ADHD; sets out onset, trajectory and mechanism as the three tests for differential diagnosis, and describes adult hyperactivity as inner restlessness.

nodes.label: Inhibitory control and psychopathology: a meta-analysis of studies using the stop signal task
nodes.venue: Journal of the International Neuropsychological Society, 16(6):1064–1076
nodes.summary: Medium stop-signal deficits across ADHD (g=0.62), OCD (g=0.77) and schizophrenia (g=0.69) — inhibition impairment is transdiagnostic, and OCD's exceeds ADHD's.

nodes.label: The Internal Restlessness Scale: performance of college students with and without ADHD
nodes.summary: Develops the Internal Restlessness Scale (IRS) to measure the mental/subjective restlessness that adults with ADHD report in place of overt motor hyperactivity; ADHD college students score significantly higher, and the scale shows a four-factor structure.

nodes.label: Practical considerations for the evaluation and management of Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) in adults
nodes.summary: Clinician-facing review of adult ADHD; notes that in adulthood hyperactivity is more often internalized and that inattention can be masked by anxiety or obsessive-like compensation — directly relevant to the internal-restlessness / anxiety differential.

nodes.label: The Internal, External, and Diagnostic Validity of Sluggish Cognitive Tempo: A Meta-Analysis and Critical Review
nodes.venue: Journal of the American Academy of Child & Adolescent Psychiatry, 55(3):163–178
nodes.summary: First meta-analysis of sluggish cognitive tempo (SCT): across >19,000 individuals 13 SCT items load on an SCT factor separable from ADHD; SCT correlates more with internalizing than with hyperactivity/impulsivity and predicts impairment — evidence for a construct distinct from ADHD inattention.

nodes.label: Report of a Work Group on Sluggish Cognitive Tempo: Key Research Directions and a Consensus Change in Terminology to Cognitive Disengagement Syndrome
nodes.venue: Journal of the American Academy of Child & Adolescent Psychiatry, 62(6):629–645
nodes.summary: Consensus paper renaming SCT to cognitive disengagement syndrome (CDS); defines it as cognitive disengagement/decoupling of attention (staring, daydreaming, mental fogginess) plus hypoactivity, empirically distinct from ADHD inattention and linked to depression, with data across the lifespan.

nodes.label: The prevalence and correlates of adult ADHD in the United States: results from the National Comorbidity Survey Replication
nodes.summary: Nationally representative US survey (NCS-R): current adult ADHD prevalence 4.4%, highly comorbid with other DSM-IV disorders and substantially impairing; most cases untreated though often treated for the comorbidities — evidence the disorder frequently hides behind its co-occurring conditions.

nodes.label: Emotion dysregulation in attention deficit hyperactivity disorder
nodes.summary: Review concluding emotion dysregulation is prevalent across the ADHD lifespan and a major source of impairment, arising from attention-to-emotion deficits in a striato-amygdalo-medial-prefrontal network; explicitly lays out three competing models of how it relates to ADHD (distinct dimension / core feature / separate entity).

nodes.label: Adult ADHD and comorbid disorders: clinical implications of a dimensional approach
nodes.summary: Review of adult ADHD comorbidity: up to 80% have a coexisting psychiatric disorder (most often mood/anxiety), overlapping symptoms complicate diagnosis, and a spectrum/dimensional framing plus treat-the-most-impairing-first is advocated; emotional dysregulation described as a distinctive attribute of adult ADHD.

nodes.label: A conceptual review of the comorbidity of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder and anxiety: implications for future research and practice
nodes.summary: Conceptual review of ADHD–anxiety comorbidity (~25% of children with ADHD have an anxiety disorder); examines methodological and substantive causes including temperament, genetics and the temporal relations between the two, and argues progress needs more precise phenotypic classification of ADHD.

nodes.label: The World Federation of ADHD International Consensus Statement: 208 Evidence-based conclusions about the disorder
nodes.summary: Consensus statement (79 authors, 27 countries) distilling ADHD evidence into 208 numbered conclusions; Conclusion 14 states ADHD can only be diagnosed by a licensed clinician via interview and not by rating scales, neuropsychological tests or imaging alone.

nodes.label: Updated European Consensus Statement on diagnosis and treatment of adult ADHD
nodes.summary: European consensus (63 experts) on adult ADHD assessment and treatment: the clinical interview is essential and covers childhood and adult symptoms/impairment; a collateral informant is of great value where retrospective recall is poor; a four-symptom adult cut-off is endorsed.

nodes.label: Accuracy of adult recall of childhood attention deficit hyperactivity disorder
nodes.summary: Prospective 16-year follow-up testing whether adults accurately recall childhood ADHD: positive predictive value of retrospective self-report was only 0.27, so most retrospective childhood diagnoses are invalid — underscoring the need for contemporaneous or collateral childhood information.

nodes.label: When diagnosing ADHD in young adults emphasize informant reports, DSM items, and impairment
nodes.venue: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology, 80(6):1052–1061
nodes.summary: Childhood-diagnosed sample (N=321) showing parent report is more diagnostically sensitive than self-report: young adults with ADHD underreport symptoms while controls overreport, with no added benefit to combining self-report with parent report — argues for weighting informants and impairment.

nodes.label: Dextroamphetamine: cognitive and behavioral effects in normal prepubertal boys
nodes.summary: Double-blind study of a single dextroamphetamine dose in 14 normal prepubertal boys: they showed reduced motor activity and improved cognitive performance just like hyperactive children, casting doubt on the idea of a stimulant response specific to ADHD — the classic evidence that medication response is not diagnostic.

nodes.label: Comparative efficacy and tolerability of medications for ADHD in children, adolescents, and adults: a systematic review and network meta-analysis
nodes.summary: Network meta-analysis of 133 double-blind RCTs across the lifespan; taking efficacy and safety together, supports methylphenidate as first choice in children/adolescents and amphetamines in adults for short-term ADHD treatment, while flagging that long-term effects are under-studied.

nodes.label: Meta-analysis of cognitive-behavioral treatments for adult ADHD
nodes.venue: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology, 85(7):737–750
nodes.summary: Meta-analysis of 32 CBT studies (up to 896 adults): medium-to-large pre-post effects and small-to-medium effects versus control, comparable to well-established behavioural treatments for children — evidence that non-pharmacological treatment meaningfully reduces adult ADHD symptoms.

nodes.label: The Effectiveness of Mindfulness-Based Therapies for ADHD: A Meta-Analytic Review
nodes.summary: Meta-analysis of mindfulness-based therapies for ADHD: moderate effect sizes for inattention (d = -.66) and hyperactivity/impulsivity (d = -.53), suggesting mindfulness is a promising adjunct — though the authors frame the benefit tentatively.

nodes.label: Spontaneous attentional fluctuations in impaired states and pathological conditions: a neurobiological hypothesis
nodes.summary: The default-mode interference hypothesis: low-frequency default-mode-network activity active during rest can intrude into task periods, producing periodic attentional lapses that compete with goal-directed behaviour — proposed as a cause of performance (reaction-time) variability in ADHD.

nodes.label: Large-scale brain systems in ADHD: beyond the prefrontal-striatal model
nodes.summary: Reframes ADHD away from a single prefrontal-striatal locus toward dysfunction distributed across multiple large-scale resting-state networks (frontoparietal, dorsal attention, motor, visual, default) — a systems-level, non-focal model of the disorder.

nodes.label: Subcortical brain volume differences in participants with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder in children and adults: a cross-sectional mega-analysis
nodes.summary: ENIGMA mega-analysis (1713 ADHD, 1529 controls, 23 sites): several subcortical volumes are smaller in ADHD but with very small effect sizes (Cohen’s d roughly -0.10 to -0.19), largest in children and negligible in adults — real group differences that are far too small to diagnose an individual.

nodes.label: Brain Imaging of the Cortex in ADHD: A Coordinated Analysis of Large-Scale Clinical and Population-Based Samples
nodes.summary: ENIGMA cortical analysis: small surface-area reductions in children with ADHD (largest effect Cohen’s d=-0.21), with no surface-area or thickness differences detected in adolescents or adults — reinforcing that structural imaging is not an individual diagnostic test, least of all in adults.

nodes.label: Shared heritability of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder and autism spectrum disorder
nodes.summary: Review of family, twin and molecular-genetic studies: ADHD and ASD co-occur at high frequency (20–50% of ADHD children meet ASD criteria; 30–80% of ASD children meet ADHD criteria) and family/twin data support partly shared familial-genetic origins, with some candidate pleiotropic genes.

nodes.label: Autism Spectrum Disorders and ADHD: Overlapping Phenomenology, Diagnostic Issues, and Treatment Considerations
nodes.summary: Review of the ASD+ADHD comorbid state: the two share genetic heritability and impairments in social and executive functioning, but differ enough in phenotypic presentation that they are held to be distinct diagnostic categories, and each must be considered when treating the other.

nodes.label: The co-occurrence of autism and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder in children — what do we know?
nodes.summary: Review of ASD–ADHD co-occurrence in children; notes that DSM-IV made an ASD diagnosis an exclusion criterion for ADHD (limiting research), that DSM-5 now permits a dual diagnosis, and that the two share phenotypic features but retain distinct diagnostic criteria.

nodes.label: Delayed circadian rhythm in adults with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder and chronic sleep-onset insomnia
nodes.summary: Actigraphy and salivary melatonin in 40 adults with ADHD: those with sleep-onset insomnia showed a delayed sleep period and delayed dim-light melatonin onset versus ADHD adults without insomnia and versus controls — objective evidence of circadian phase delay in the majority of adult ADHD with insomnia.

nodes.label: The role of the circadian system in the etiology and pathophysiology of ADHD: time to redefine ADHD?
nodes.venue: ADHD Attention Deficit and Hyperactivity Disorders, 11(1):5–19
nodes.summary: Review arguing delayed sleep phase disorder is present in 73–78% of people with ADHD, that ADHD may be cause, consequence, or shared-etiology with sleep disturbance, and proposing that part of ADHD symptomatology results from chronic circadian delay — a possible redefinition of a subgroup.

nodes.label: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder in adolescence predicts onset of major depressive disorder through early adulthood
nodes.summary: Longitudinal Oregon Adolescent Depression Project (N=1507): a lifetime history of ADHD in mid-adolescence predicted onset of major depression through age 30, and the effect survived adjustment for gender, other disorders, impairment and coping (hazard ratio 1.81) — ADHD as a robust prospective risk factor for depression.

nodes.label: ADHD and depression: investigating a causal explanation
nodes.summary: Combines a longitudinal cohort (ALSPAC, N=8310) with two-sample Mendelian randomization: childhood ADHD predicted recurrent young-adult depression, and genetic liability for ADHD showed a causal effect on major depression — evidence the ADHD→depression link is partly causal, not only correlational.

nodes.label: Prospective follow-up of girls with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder into early adulthood: continuing impairment includes elevated risk for suicide attempts and self-injury
nodes.venue: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology, 80(6):1041–1051
nodes.summary: The Berkeley Girls with ADHD Longitudinal Study: a 10-year follow-up of 140 childhood-diagnosed girls plus 88 comparisons. Girls with ADHD showed persistent symptoms, serious impairment, and markedly higher rates of suicide attempts and self-injury, with effect sizes up to very large — evidence that ADHD in girls is far from benign.

nodes.label: Females with ADHD: An expert consensus statement taking a lifespan approach providing guidance for the identification and treatment of ADHD in girls and women
nodes.summary: UK expert-consensus statement on females with ADHD across the lifespan: the male:female diagnostic ratio partly reflects lack of recognition and referral bias, females differ in symptom profile, comorbidity and functioning, and practical guidance is offered to improve identification and treatment.

nodes.label: Reproductive steroids and ADHD symptoms across the menstrual cycle
nodes.summary: Daily-diary study of 32 regularly-cycling young women: lower estradiol combined with higher progesterone or testosterone predicted higher next-day ADHD symptoms, especially in high-impulsivity women, with symptom peaks in the early follicular and early luteal phases — evidence that ADHD expression tracks reproductive-hormone fluctuations.

nodes.label: Behavioral inhibition, sustained attention, and executive functions: constructing a unifying theory of ADHD
nodes.summary: The influential theoretical model casting ADHD as a primary deficit in behavioral inhibition, from which four executive functions (working memory, self-regulation of affect/motivation/arousal, internalization of speech, reconstitution) secondarily follow. Foundational to the executive-function theory of ADHD.

nodes.label: Predicting impairment in major life activities and occupational functioning in hyperactive children as adults: self-reported executive function (EF) deficits versus EF tests
nodes.summary: Longitudinal follow-up (hyperactive N=135, controls N=75) to adulthood comparing self-reported EF deficits against EF tests: the ratings predicted impairment in major life activities and occupational functioning far better than the tests did, most of which were unrelated to work history — an ecological-validity gap between real-world EF and lab EF.

nodes.label: Implications of rejection sensitivity for intimate relationships
nodes.venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 70(6):1327–1343
nodes.summary: The foundational operationalisation of rejection sensitivity as a general cognitive-affective disposition to anxiously expect, readily perceive, and overreact to rejection; four studies link it to dissatisfaction and conflict in intimate relationships. Not ADHD-specific — the established construct that predates the ADHD label.

nodes.label: Rejection sensitivity dysphoria: a critical reflection
nodes.summary: Critical reflection in the Dutch journal of psychiatry on "rejection sensitivity dysphoria" (RSD): a social-media-popularised term coined by William Dodson from clinical experience, whose clinical use carries four risks — self-stigmatisation, framing as innate, terminological confusion, and limited empirical evidence — with the established rejection-sensitivity spectrum offered as the better alternative.

nodes.label: The lived experience of rejection sensitivity in ADHD — A qualitative exploration
nodes.summary: Small qualitative focus-group study (five undergraduates) framing rejection sensitivity as an under-explored aspect of ADHD-related emotional dysregulation; thematic analysis surfaced withdrawal, masking, and bodily sensations. Illustrative of the phenomenon and of how thin and early-stage the ADHD-specific evidence still is.

nodes.label: Living "in the zone": hyperfocus in adult ADHD
nodes.venue: ADHD Attention Deficit and Hyperactivity Disorders, 11(2):191–208
nodes.summary: Introduces the Adult Hyperfocus Questionnaire and tests, across a pilot (n=251) and replication (n=372) sample, whether hyperfocus rises with ADHD symptomology: those with higher ADHD symptoms reported more hyperfocus across school, hobbies, screen time and real-world scenarios — the first comprehensive assessment of a "potentially separable feature" of ADHD.

nodes.label: Hyperfocus: the forgotten frontier of attention
nodes.summary: Conceptual review of hyperfocus — complete task absorption with tuning-out of everything else — arguing it is poorly and inconsistently defined, most often invoked for autism, schizophrenia and ADHD but with limited research on its cognitive/neural basis; proposes an operational definition. The critical, evidence-appraisal counterweight.

nodes.label: Hyperfocusing as a dimension of adult attention deficit hyperactivity disorder
nodes.summary: Case-control study (ADHD stimulant-naive n=53, on stimulants n=79, controls n=65) using a Hyperfocusing Scale: hyperfocusing scores were higher in ADHD than controls and did not differ by stimulant use, supporting hyperfocusing as a separate dimension of adult ADHD and reframing it as an inability to shift attention as well as to focus.

nodes.label: Timing deficits in attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD): evidence from neurocognitive and neuroimaging studies
nodes.summary: Integrative review of timing in ADHD across neurocognitive and neuroimaging studies, concluding ADHD is consistently impaired in three timing domains — motor timing, perceptual timing and temporal foresight — across timescales from milliseconds to years.

nodes.label: Clinical Implications of the Perception of Time in Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD): A Review
nodes.summary: Review of time perception in ADHD emphasising the clinical/lived side: difficulties in time estimation and discrimination plus the felt sense that time slips away without tasks being completed well; proposes impaired time perception as a possible diagnostic characteristic.

nodes.label: Temporal information processing in ADHD: findings to date and new methods
nodes.summary: Review of temporal information processing in ADHD: growing but still-to-be-replicated evidence of problems in duration discrimination, duration reproduction and finger tapping, implicating cerebellar, basal-ganglia and prefrontal substrates — framing timing as a more basic cognitive mechanism than usually linked to ADHD.

nodes.label: Motivation deficit in ADHD is associated with dysfunction of the dopamine reward pathway
nodes.summary: PET study of 45 adults with ADHD vs 41 controls: decreased dopamine reward-pathway function (D2/D3 receptors and transporters in accumbens/midbrain) correlated with lower trait motivation in ADHD but not controls — direct neurobiological evidence linking a motivation deficit to reward-pathway dysfunction.

nodes.label: The impact of reinforcement contingencies on AD/HD: a review and theoretical appraisal
nodes.summary: Review of 22 studies (N=1181 children) on reinforcement and ADHD: an aberrant sensitivity to reinforcement is proposed as a core deficit; reward improves task performance and motivation (somewhat more in ADHD), high-intensity reinforcement is effective, and children with ADHD prefer immediate over delayed reward.

nodes.label: What motivates individuals with ADHD? A qualitative analysis from the adolescent’s point of view
nodes.summary: Qualitative interview study of adolescents with and without ADHD: motivational themes were largely shared across groups, but individuals with ADHD respond differently to incentives, consistent with an altered sensitivity to reinforcers and possibly qualitatively different motivators.

nodes.label: A meta-analysis of working memory impairments in children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder
nodes.venue: Journal of the American Academy of Child & Adolescent Psychiatry, 44(4):377–384
nodes.summary: Meta-analysis of 26 studies: children with ADHD show deficits across multiple working-memory components, independent of language-learning comorbidity and IQ, with larger effect sizes for spatial working memory (storage ~0.85, central executive ~1.06) than verbal (~0.43–0.47).

nodes.label: Moderators of working memory deficits in children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD): a meta-analytic review
nodes.summary: Meta-analytic review finding large between-group working-memory deficits across phonological and visuospatial domains, with task and sample moderators explaining effect-size heterogeneity; frames working memory as a prominent candidate primary deficit/endophenotype in ADHD models.

nodes.label: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and working memory in adults: a meta-analytic review
nodes.summary: First meta-analysis of working memory in adults with ADHD (38 studies): moderate-magnitude deficits across phonological and visuospatial domains that persist into adulthood, with methodological variability explaining why deficits are not uniformly detected.

nodes.label: Hyperactivity in Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD): Impairing Deficit or Compensatory Behavior?
nodes.summary: Objective study of gross motor activity during working-memory tasks in boys with ADHD (n=29) vs controls (n=23): higher activity predicted significantly better (though not normalised) working-memory performance in ADHD, but somewhat worse performance in typically developing children — evidence that hyperactivity may be partly compensatory.

nodes.label: Atypical sensory profiles as core features of adult ADHD, irrespective of autistic symptoms
nodes.summary: 116 adults with ADHD completed the Adolescent/Adult Sensory Profile and Autism-spectrum Quotient: they showed both more hyper- and hyposensitivity than norms (especially auditory and activity-level), with a dose-response relationship to ADHD severity, present irrespective of autistic symptoms.

nodes.label: Sensory processing problems in children with ADHD, a systematic review
nodes.summary: Systematic review (11 ADHD studies): sensory processing problems are more common in children with ADHD than in typically developing children, do not distinguish ADHD subtypes, and are worse with comorbid ODD/anxiety — while noting the area is not well studied.

nodes.label: The relationship between ADHD traits and sensory sensitivity in the general population
nodes.summary: Online study of 234 adults: ADHD traits correlated highly with the frequency of sensory processing problems across all modalities, ADHD traits predicted sensory difficulties, and a factor combined ADHD-trait and sensory items — the first general-population evidence that sensory difficulty tracks ADHD traits dimensionally.

nodes.label: Prospective association of childhood attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and substance use and abuse/dependence: a meta-analytic review
nodes.summary: Meta-analysis of longitudinal studies following children with and without ADHD into adolescence/adulthood: childhood ADHD predicted later abuse/dependence for nicotine, alcohol, marijuana, cocaine and other substances — prospective evidence that ADHD is an early risk factor for substance disorders.

nodes.label: Prevalence of attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder in substance use disorder patients: a meta-analysis and meta-regression analysis
nodes.summary: Meta-analysis of 29 studies: about 23% of substance-use-disorder patients meet criteria for comorbid ADHD (varying by substance and assessment method) — the reciprocal of the ADHD-to-SUD risk, showing ADHD is heavily over-represented in addiction populations.

nodes.label: The self-esteem of adults diagnosed with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD): a systematic review of the literature
nodes.venue: ADHD Attention Deficit and Hyperactivity Disorders, 6(4):249–268
nodes.summary: Systematic review of 13 studies on self-esteem in adults with ADHD: adults with ADHD, who often grow up with negative messages about their abilities, show lower self-esteem, and these difficulties can be at least partly remedied by psychotherapeutic work.

nodes.label: Long-Term Outcomes of ADHD: A Systematic Review of Self-Esteem and Social Function
nodes.summary: Systematic review of 127 studies on long-term (≥2 year) outcomes: untreated ADHD was associated with poorer self-esteem and social function than non-ADHD controls, and treatment (pharmacological or not) was associated with improvement in the majority of self-esteem outcomes.

nodes.label: Self-esteem evaluation in children and adolescents suffering from ADHD
nodes.venue: Clinical Practice & Epidemiology in Mental Health, 9:96–102
nodes.summary: Case-control study (85 ADHD youth, 26 controls) using a multidimensional self-esteem test: ADHD subjects scored lower on all self-esteem domains, with far higher rates in the pathological range than controls, drug-free and drug-treated alike.

nodes.label: The marital and family functioning of adults with ADHD and their spouses
nodes.summary: Compared 33 married adults with ADHD and their spouses to 26 control couples: adults with ADHD reported poorer marital adjustment and more family dysfunction than controls, viewed their marriages more negatively than their spouses did, and their spouses often compensated for their difficulties — underscoring the need to address marital/family functioning in treatment.

nodes.label: Rate and predictors of divorce among parents of youths with ADHD
nodes.venue: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology, 76(5):735–744
nodes.summary: Survival analysis comparing parents of youths with (n=282) and without (n=206) childhood ADHD: parents of youths with ADHD were more likely to divorce and divorced sooner, with several parent and child variables predicting the timing — evidence that ADHD in the family strains couple relationships.

nodes.label: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder symptom levels and romantic relationship quality in college students
nodes.summary: Survey of 189 undergraduates: those with clinically significant hyperactive-impulsive and inattentive symptoms reported lower romantic relationship quality than non-ADHD peers, an association mediated by emotion-regulation problems and hostile relationship conflict.

nodes.label: Adult ADHD and romantic relationships: What we know and what we can do to help
nodes.venue: Journal of Marital and Family Therapy, 47(3):664–681
nodes.summary: Narrative review of romantic relationships in adults with ADHD: converging evidence that they are shorter-lived and more discordant, a survey of the distal and proximal factors that raise relationship-distress risk, and an argument that research on what would strengthen these relationships — and so on prevention and intervention — is underdeveloped.

nodes.label: Young adult romantic couples' conflict resolution and satisfaction varies with partner's attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder type
nodes.venue: Journal of Marital and Family Therapy, 40(4):509–524
nodes.summary: Observational study of young-adult couples with a conflict-resolution task coded via the Rapid Couples Interaction Scoring System: combined-type ADHD couples showed more negativity and less positivity — tracking lower satisfaction — while inattentive-type couples behaved much like non-diagnosed couples, locating the observable conflict signature in the combined presentation.

nodes.label: Prevalence of sexual dysfunctions and other sexual disorders in adults with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder compared to the general population
nodes.venue: ADHD Attention Deficit and Hyperactivity Disorders, 10(1):87–96
nodes.summary: Survey of 136 adults in a Dutch ADHD clinic screened against two large general-population surveys: 39% of men and 43% of women with ADHD screened positive for a sexual dysfunction, and a further 17%/5% for another sexual disorder — far above population rates and almost never previously diagnosed — supporting routine screening for sexual problems during ADHD assessment.

nodes.label: ADHD Symptomology and Social Functioning in College Students
nodes.summary: Regression study of emerging adults: higher ADHD symptomology predicted greater social impairment and higher state and trait anger, but not lower romantic-relationship satisfaction or intimate-partner-violence rates — a mixed result that tempers the couple-level findings and points to anger and social skills as treatment targets.

nodes.label: The effects of physical exercise in children with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized control trials
nodes.summary: Meta-analysis of 8 RCTs (n=249): aerobic exercise had a moderate-to-large effect on core ADHD symptoms — attention (SMD 0.84), hyperactivity (0.56) and impulsivity (0.56) — in children and adolescents.

nodes.label: Sweat it out? The effects of physical exercise on cognition and behavior in children and adults with ADHD: a systematic literature review
nodes.summary: Systematic review of physical exercise in ADHD organised by exercise type, acute versus chronic effect, and outcome: cardio exercise is acutely beneficial for executive functions (e.g., impulsivity), response time and physical measures, with beneficial chronic effects as well.

nodes.label: The Effects of Physical Exercise on Functional Outcomes in the Treatment of ADHD: A Meta-Analysis
nodes.summary: Meta-analysis of 10 studies of exercise effects on motor skills and executive functions in children with ADHD: a significant overall effect (g=0.627), larger with longer intervention duration and unrelated to intensity, age or gender — a modest, dose-dependent benefit.

nodes.label: Meta-analysis of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder or attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder symptoms, restriction diet, and synthetic food color additives
nodes.venue: Journal of the American Academy of Child & Adolescent Psychiatry, 51(1):86–97
nodes.summary: Meta-analysis of restriction diets (g=0.29) and synthetic food colors (parent-rated g=0.18, falling to 0.12 after publication-bias correction): a restriction diet benefits some children, while food-color effects are small and susceptible to bias — modest, subgroup-specific dietary effects.

nodes.label: Omega-3 fatty acid supplementation for the treatment of children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder symptomatology: systematic review and meta-analysis
nodes.venue: Journal of the American Academy of Child & Adolescent Psychiatry, 50(10):991–1000
nodes.summary: Meta-analysis of 10 RCTs (699 children): omega-3 supplementation, especially higher-EPA formulations, was modestly effective for ADHD symptoms — less than standard pharmacotherapy, but with a benign side-effect profile, reasonable as augmentation or where medication is declined.

nodes.label: The effect of sugar on behavior or cognition in children. A meta-analysis
nodes.summary: Meta-analysis of 23 blinded, placebo-controlled sugar-challenge studies: sugar did not affect the behaviour or cognition of children, with the strong parental belief attributed to expectancy and association — the classic debunking of the sugar-causes-hyperactivity myth.

nodes.label: Media use and ADHD-related behaviors in children and adolescents: A meta-analysis
nodes.summary: Meta-analysis of 45 studies on media use and ADHD-related behaviors (attention problems, hyperactivity, impulsivity): a small but significant overall relationship (r+ = .12), after decades of inconsistent findings.

nodes.label: Association of Digital Media Use With Subsequent Symptoms of Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder Among Adolescents
nodes.summary: Prospective cohort of 2,587 adolescents without significant ADHD symptoms at baseline, followed 24 months: higher-frequency digital media use was associated with a statistically significant but modest increase in subsequent ADHD symptoms, with causality left open.

nodes.label: Screen media use and ADHD-related behaviors: Four decades of research
nodes.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 115(40):9875–9881
nodes.summary: Systematic review of four decades of research on screen media use and ADHD-related behaviors: the evidence indicates a statistically small relationship, moderated by individual child differences, with a clear need for research on causality and mechanisms.

nodes.label: The relation between procrastination and symptoms of attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) in undergraduate students
nodes.venue: International Journal of Methods in Psychiatric Research, 23(4):411–421
nodes.summary: Study of 54 undergraduates across a range of ADHD-related behaviour: procrastination is often targeted in ADHD psychotherapy but is not a formal ADHD symptom; after correcting for the other domain, only inattention (not impulsivity) correlated with general procrastination.

nodes.label: Academic procrastination in college students: the role of self-reported executive function
nodes.venue: Journal of Clinical and Experimental Neuropsychology, 33(3):344–357
nodes.summary: Study of 212 college students framing procrastination as self-regulation/volition failure: executive-function domains — initiation, plan/organize, inhibit, self-monitor, working memory, task monitor, organization of materials — significantly predicted academic procrastination, over and above IQ, mood and conscientiousness.

nodes.label: The nature of procrastination: a meta-analytic and theoretical review of quintessential self-regulatory failure
nodes.summary: Meta-analysis of 691 correlations on procrastination: its strong, consistent predictors are task aversiveness, task delay, low self-efficacy and impulsiveness (plus low conscientiousness, self-control, distractibility), consistent with temporal motivation theory built on hyperbolic discounting — a general self-regulatory failure.

nodes.label: Stigma in attention deficit hyperactivity disorder
nodes.venue: ADHD Attention Deficit and Hyperactivity Disorders, 4(3):101–114
nodes.summary: Review of empirical research on ADHD stigma across children, adults and relatives: people with ADHD are at high risk of stigma, prejudice and discrimination, with contributors including public uncertainty about the validity of the ADHD diagnosis, perceived dangerousness, and skepticism toward ADHD medication.

nodes.label: Internalized stigma, anticipated discrimination and perceived public stigma in adults with ADHD
nodes.venue: ADHD Attention Deficit and Hyperactivity Disorders, 11(2):211–220
nodes.summary: Survey of 104 adults with ADHD: 23% reported high internalized stigma, 89% anticipated discrimination and 69% perceived public stigma; stigma correlated with symptoms, distress, self-esteem, impairment and quality of life, and the most frequent stereotype was doubt about the validity of ADHD as a disorder.

nodes.label: Stigmatization of ADHD: A Developmental Review
nodes.summary: Developmental review of ADHD stigma across ages of target and perceiver: nationally representative, experimental, survey and qualitative evidence indicates people of all ages with ADHD symptoms face substantial stigmatization, present throughout development.

nodes.label: Effect of melatonin on sleep, behavior, and cognition in ADHD and chronic sleep-onset insomnia
nodes.venue: Journal of the American Academy of Child & Adolescent Psychiatry, 46(2):233–241
nodes.summary: RCT of melatonin in 105 medication-free children with ADHD and chronic sleep-onset insomnia: melatonin advanced sleep onset (~27 min) and dim-light melatonin onset and increased total sleep versus placebo, but had no significant effect on behavior, cognition or quality of life — it fixes sleep timing, not ADHD symptoms.

nodes.label: Impact of a behavioural sleep intervention on symptoms and sleep in children with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, and parental mental health: randomised controlled trial
nodes.summary: RCT of a brief sleep-hygiene plus behavioural sleep intervention in 244 children with ADHD: the intervention reduced ADHD symptom severity at three and six months and roughly halved moderate-severe sleep problems, with about a half to a third of the symptom benefit mediated through improved sleep.

nodes.label: Strategies for Coping with Time-Related and Productivity Challenges of Young People with Learning Disabilities and Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder
nodes.summary: Qualitative study of 52 college students with LD/ADHD: they must work longer and harder than peers, and the coping strategies they use for time and productivity fall into habit/routine use, reframing, and symptom-specific strategies — a multidimensional mix of cognitive and behavioural tactics.

nodes.label: Cognitive-behavioral therapy for ADHD in medication-treated adults with continued symptoms
nodes.summary: RCT of a skills-based CBT (organisation, planning, coping) added to stable medication in 31 adults with ADHD and residual symptoms: the CBT group had significantly lower clinician- and self-rated ADHD symptoms, global severity, anxiety and depression than medication alone — coping skills add benefit beyond medication.

nodes.label: Long-term effects of cognitive behavioural therapy on the quality of life in adult ADHD
nodes.summary: Long-term (4–8 year) follow-up of 159 adults who had received CBT plus pharmacotherapy and psychoeducation: no significant added effect of CBT on quality of life over time — the delayed skill-building/coping benefit hypothesised for quality of life was not confirmed.

nodes.label: Prevalence of hormone-related mood disorder symptoms in women with ADHD
nodes.summary: First study of hormone-related mood conditions across reproductive events in 209 women with ADHD: premenstrual dysphoric disorder and postpartum depression symptoms were more prevalent than in the general population, with elevated climacteric anxiety, depression and vasomotor complaints.

nodes.label: Cognitive functions of regularly cycling women may differ throughout the month, depending on sex hormone status; a possible explanation to conflicting results of studies of ADHD in females
nodes.summary: Review arguing sex hormones regulate intracellular signalling systems thought to be abnormal in ADHD, so hormone status across the menstrual cycle may shape the clinical picture in women — and that treating the cycle as a nuisance or testing only males has muddied the female-ADHD literature.

nodes.label: Research advances and future directions in female ADHD: the lifelong interplay of hormonal fluctuations with mood, cognition, and disease
nodes.summary: Eunethydis Special Interest Group review of female ADHD across the lifespan, framing the lifelong interplay of hormonal fluctuations with mood, cognition and disease, and highlighting late diagnosis, puberty, hormonal birth control, executive-function difficulties and associated gynaecological disorders.

nodes.label: Creativity and ADHD: A review of behavioral studies, the effect of psychostimulants and neural underpinnings
nodes.summary: Review of 31 behavioral studies on creativity and ADHD: increased divergent thinking appears mainly at subclinical (high-trait) rather than clinical levels, creative abilities/achievements are high in both, there is no convergent-thinking advantage, and psychostimulants do not overall reduce creativity.

nodes.label: Creativity in ADHD: Goal-Directed Motivation and Domain Specificity
nodes.summary: Two studies of adults with ADHD: they reported more real-world creative achievements and generated more original ideas when competing for a bonus, suggesting goal-directed motivation drives their creative achievement and that they selectively excel in self-chosen creative domains.

nodes.label: Behavioral models of impulsivity in relation to ADHD: translation between clinical and preclinical studies
nodes.summary: Review arguing impulsivity (action without foresight) is not a unitary construct but a set of related phenomena with different biological bases, fractionated by distinct paradigms (five-choice serial reaction time, stop-signal, delay-discounting); relevant across ADHD, mania and substance abuse.

nodes.label: Annual Research Review: On the relations among self-regulation, self-control, executive functioning, effortful control, cognitive control, impulsivity, risk-taking, and inhibition for developmental psychopathology
nodes.venue: Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry, 58(4):361–383
nodes.summary: Conceptual review untangling the overlapping terms around self-regulation, arguing for a domain-general self-regulation construct spanning action, emotion and cognition with both top-down and bottom-up processes — situating impulsivity as dysregulation of action within a broader, multi-domain self-regulation framework.
